title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 physical education (PE) teachers perceive the opportunities and challenges of integrating artificial intelligence into their classes. The authors note that while AI has been widely discussed in education, PE remains underexplored despite its distinctive instructional demands, such as large open spaces, safety monitoring, individualized feedback, and multi-dimensional assessment.

To explore these issues, the study conducted in-person focus group ideation workshops with 17 in-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea. Participants first discussed their classroom challenges, then received short instructional introductions to basic AI capabilities and ideated potential AI-supported solutions through sketching, storyboarding, and role-playing. The workshop format was designed to surface both envisioned uses of AI and the concerns teachers had about adoption and implementation.

Teachers envisioned AI in four broad supportive roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. Across these roles, they imagined AI helping with class management, personalized feedback, balanced team formation, and assessment automation. At the same time, participants raised concerns about institutional support, infrastructure, teacher technology readiness, pedagogical misalignment, overuse and overreliance, and student data privacy. The paper concludes that AI should support rather than replace teachers and that successful integration in PE requires alignment with pedagogical goals, robust infrastructure, and careful attention to ethical and practical constraints.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / AI chatbot or AI system concept used for instructional support, feedback, class management, and evaluation; no specific commercial product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is an ideation-workshop study in which 17 in-service K-12 secondary physical education teachers envisioned possible AI roles in PE classes (operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, evaluator) and discussed benefits and concerns.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative ideation/workshop study with 17 teachers, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It provides useful user-perspective evidence but no outcome testing or causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measured effects on student or teacher outcomes, so there is no demonstrated positive or negative impact. It does surface important implementation concerns such as overreliance, privacy, and pedagogical misalignment, but these are anticipatory rather than observed impacts.
